1.title: Diffraction
1.text:
Diffraction

Diffraction is the bending of light as it passes the edge of a barrier.

Our big question for this lesson: how do scientists use the Doppler shift to determine how stars and galaxies are moving? Let's ride the light wave!

In 1665, Italian scientist Francesco Maria Grimaldi noticed that shadow edges aren't perfectly sharp. He let a narrow beam of light into a dark room and held a rod in front of it to cast a shadow on a white surface. The shadow was wider than it should have been if light traveled in perfectly straight lines past the rod's edges. And it was bordered by colored bands!

Grimaldi realized both observations made sense if light bent slightly. He called the bending of light as it passes the edge of a barrier diffraction.

3.title: Huygens' Principle
3.text:
Huygens' Principle

Huygens' principle states that all points on a wavefront can be thought of as new sources of smaller waves, called wavelets.

In 1678, Dutch scientist Christiaan Huygens used a wave model to explain diffraction. By Huygens' principle, every point on a wavefront of light acts as a new source of smaller waves. These wavelets spread out in every direction, all in step with one another. A flat, or plane, wavefront is made of an endless number of point sources in a line.

In Figure 12, the wavelets combine to form a straight wavefront, except at the edges. When a wavefront passes an edge, the edge cuts it off, and the wavelets from the points near the edge spread out as circular waves into the region behind the barrier. That's how the wave model explained Grimaldi's diffraction.

4.title: Newton's Prism and Color
4.text:
Newton's Prism and Color

A spectrum is the ordered arrangement of colors produced when white light is separated.

In 1666, Isaac Newton passed a narrow beam of sunlight through a glass prism and saw colors, as in Figure 13. He called the ordered band of colors a spectrum. Using his particle model of light, later disproved, he first thought light particles were interacting with some unevenness in the glass.

To test it, Newton sent the spectrum from one prism into a second prism. If glass irregularities caused the colors, the second prism should spread them even more. Instead, it reversed the spreading and recombined the colors into white light! Newton concluded that white light is made of colors, and that some property of the glass other than unevenness separates them.

5.title: Color and Wavelength
5.text:
Color and Wavelength

Visible light has wavelengths from about 400 nanometers to 700 nanometers.

Can the wave model explain Newton's colors? A wave needs a wavelength and a frequency. Work by Grimaldi, Huygens, Newton, and others suggested that color is tied to wavelength. Visible light runs from about 400 nanometers, or 4.00 times ten to the negative seventh meters, to 700 nanometers, or 7.00 times ten to the negative seventh meters. The longest wavelengths look red, and the shortest look violet.

When white light passes from air into glass and back out, each color bends by a different angle. The shorter the wavelength, the more it bends. That uneven bending spreads white light into a spectrum.

6.title: Color by Addition
6.text:
Color by Addition

The primary colors of light are red, green, and blue; complementary colors are two colors of light that combine to make white light.

You can make white light from colored light! Shine the right intensities of red, green, and blue light on a white screen, as in Figure 14, and you get white. That's the additive color process, used in many TV screens. Red, green, and blue are the primary colors of light.

Mix them in pairs, and you get the secondary colors. Red and green make yellow, blue and green make cyan, and red and blue make magenta. These differ a bit from the primary colors you learned in art class, and we'll see why soon.

Complementary colors are two colors of light that combine to make white. Yellow light is red plus green, so adding blue gives white. Yellow and blue are complementary. So are cyan and red, and magenta and green. That's why a bluing agent in detergent can make yellowish laundry look white.

7.title: Color by Subtraction and Dyes
7.text:
Color by Subtraction and Dyes

A dye is a molecule that absorbs certain wavelengths of light and transmits or reflects others.

Objects reflect, transmit, and absorb light. An object's color depends on which wavelengths shine on it and which it absorbs or reflects. Dyes in a material, or pigments on its surface, give it color.

Dyes can come from plants or insects. Purple dye comes from black mulberry berries, yellow from the saffron crocus, and one red dye from an insect called the cochineal. A dye molecule absorbs certain wavelengths and transmits or reflects the rest. Absorbed light's energy is transformed into other forms of energy.

A red shirt looks red because its dyes reflect mostly red light. In Figure 15, white light falls on a red object, which absorbs most of the blue and green and reflects mostly red. Under blue light, the red object reflects very little and looks almost black. And the die that looks yellow in white light? Yellow reflects red and green, so in red light, it reflects red and looks red. So color by addition mixes light sources, while color by subtraction removes colors by absorbing them.

8.title: Pigments
8.text:
Pigments

A primary pigment absorbs one primary color of light and reflects two; a secondary pigment absorbs two primary colors and reflects one.

Pigments are usually crushed minerals, not plant or insect extracts. Hematite makes a red pigment, and azurite a blue one. You can even see pigment particles under a microscope. Yellow, cyan, and magenta are the primary pigments. Yellow pigment, for example, absorbs blue light and reflects red and green.

The secondary pigments are red, which absorbs green and blue, green, which absorbs red and blue, and blue, which absorbs red and green. Notice the swap: the primary pigments are light's secondary colors, and the secondary pigments are light's primary colors!

Mix yellow and cyan, as in Figure 16: yellow absorbs blue, and cyan absorbs red, so only green is left. Mix yellow with blue pigment, and all three primary colors are absorbed, so you get black. Yellow and blue are complementary pigments, as are cyan and red, and magenta and green. A color printer uses yellow, magenta, and cyan dots. Pigments like titanium(IV) oxide, which is white, chromium(III) oxide, which is green, and cadmium sulfide, which is yellow, form suspensions, not solutions, so they keep absorbing and reflecting the same wavelengths.

9.title: Why Plants Are Green
9.text:
Why Plants Are Green

Chlorophyll in green leaves reflects mostly green light, giving the leaves their color.

Now look at Figure 17. The plants on the mountain look green because of chlorophyll. Chlorophyll absorbs mostly red and blue light and reflects green. Plants use the energy of that absorbed red and blue light in photosynthesis to make food.

Why so many shades of green? Different plants hold different amounts and types of pigment, so each reflects a slightly different mix of light.

10.title: Polarization by Filtering
10.text:
Polarization by Filtering

Polarization is the production of light with a specific pattern of oscillation.

Ever looked at light reflecting off a road through polarizing sunglasses? Rotate them, and the road goes dark, light, then dark again. Lamplight barely changes. Why? Normal lamplight isn't polarized, but light reflected from the road is.

Light is a transverse wave, and what oscillates is the electric field. When that field oscillates in random directions, the light is nonpolarized. In Figure 18, the lines on the polarizer show its polarizing axis. The part of the electric field parallel to the axis passes through, and the part perpendicular is absorbed. Put a polarizer in nonpolarized light, and half of the light gets through.

How does it work? A polarizing material has long molecules whose electrons can move back and forth along them. Those electrons absorb light oscillating in their direction. The polarizing axis is perpendicular to the long molecules, and only light oscillating parallel to that axis passes through.

11.title: Polarization by Reflection and Malus's Law
11.text:
Polarization by Reflection and Malus's Law

Malus's law states that the intensity of light from a second polarizing filter equals the intensity from the first filter times the square of the cosine of the angle between their axes.

Look at light reflected from glass through a polarizing filter and rotate the filter. The light brightens and dims, because reflected light is partially polarized parallel to the glass. That polarized reflection is glare. Polarizing sunglasses cut road glare, and photographers put polarizing filters on lenses to block reflections, as in Figure 19.

Now stack two polarizing filters, as in Figure 20. With axes parallel, light passes through. With axes perpendicular, no light gets through. At 45 degrees, some passes. Call the intensity after the first filter I sub 1 and after the second I sub 2. If theta is 0, I sub 2 equals I sub 1, and if theta is 90 degrees, I sub 2 is 0. That hints at the cosine, but the real relationship is the cosine squared.

Malus's law: I sub 2 equals I sub 1 times the square of the cosine of theta. At 45 degrees, the cosine is about 0.707, and its square is one-half, so half of the light gets through the second filter.

12.title: Speed, Wavelength, and Frequency of Light
12.text:
Speed, Wavelength, and Frequency of Light

In a vacuum, the wavelength of light equals the speed of light divided by its frequency.

A wave's source sets its frequency, f, and the medium and frequency together set its wavelength, lambda. Light has wave properties, so the same math applies. In a vacuum, lambda equals c divided by f. All colors travel at c in a vacuum, but with different wavelengths, so once you measure a frequency, you can find the wavelength.

Lasers, developed in the 1960s, gave new ways to measure light. With lasers and atomic clocks, frequency can be measured with extreme precision, while wavelength measurements are much less precise.

What if a light source moves toward you? For sound, the pitch you hear changes when the source or listener moves, relative to the air. Light also shifts, but light isn't a vibration of a medium. So for light, only the relative velocity between the source and observer matters.

13.title: The Doppler Effect for Light
13.text:
The Doppler Effect for Light

The observed frequency of light equals the source frequency times the quantity 1 plus or minus the relative axial speed divided by the speed of light.

Only the velocity components along the line between source and observer count, as in Figure 21. When that relative speed is much less than the speed of light, the observed frequency is f sub obs equals f times the quantity 1 plus or minus v over c. Use plus when they move toward each other, and minus when they move apart.

Astronomers usually think in wavelengths. Using lambda equals c over f, the Doppler shift, delta lambda, is the observed wavelength minus the actual wavelength: delta lambda equals plus or minus lambda times v over c.

If the source moves away, delta lambda is positive. The observed wavelength is longer, shifted toward red. That's a red shift. If the source moves toward you, delta lambda is negative and the wavelength is shorter. That's a blue shift. A red shift means a lower observed frequency, and a blue shift means a higher one.

14.title: Reading Galaxies with Light
14.text:
Reading Galaxies with Light

A red shift shows a light source moving away from the observer; a blue shift shows it moving toward the observer.

Astronomers measure how galaxies move by studying the Doppler shift of their light. A spectrometer spreads out light from a galaxy's stars, as in Figure 22. The same elements glow at specific wavelengths in labs on Earth, so comparing the two tells astronomers how fast an object moves toward or away from us. In Figure 22, the hydrogen lines are red shifted, so that source is moving away from Earth.

In 1929, Edwin Hubble studied light from many galaxies, like the one in Figure 23. Light from familiar elements had longer wavelengths than expected. No matter where he looked, almost all galaxies were red shifted. Hubble concluded they are moving away from Earth and proposed that the universe is expanding, and later studies support this. As galaxies move, they sometimes collide and merge, with results depending on their size and speed.

Photographers use these ideas every day, composing shots with light and using polarizing filters to cut glare. Some features of light fit a simple ray model, others need the wave model, and you can use both to study mirrors and lenses.

15.title: Super-Efficient Solar Cells
15.text:
Super-Efficient Solar Cells

A photovoltaic cell converts light into electric current.

Solar panels on homes and businesses turn energy from the Sun into electricity. A panel is made of many photovoltaic, or PV, cells. Light strikes a semiconductor, usually silicon, and transfers energy to electrons, which flow in one direction to make a current.

The Sun gives off energy across the electromagnetic spectrum, but a silicon cell can use only part of it. The rest is wasted, so typical home panels convert only about 15 to 22 percent of incoming energy into electricity and need large areas, especially in cold, cloudy places.

Scientists developed solar thermophotovoltaic cells, called hot solar cells. An absorbing layer of carbon nanotubes turns sunlight into thermal energy, reaching up to 1000 degrees Celsius! Then an emitting layer of nanophotonic crystals turns that energy back into light at just the wavelengths a regular PV cell absorbs best. Early lab tests showed the idea works, and researchers hope the design could someday beat the efficiency limit of ordinary cells, which could reduce our dependence on fossil fuels.

So, how do scientists use the Doppler shift to tell how stars and galaxies move? They compare the wavelengths of light from known elements in a star or galaxy with lab wavelengths. A red shift means it's moving away, a blue shift means it's moving toward us, and the size of the shift, delta lambda equals lambda times v over c, gives the speed.
